The discovery of a novel phenomenon called stress-induced superconductivity, where increased pressure enhances the superconducting transition temperature, has been largely limited to a few materials. We have now observed stress-induced superconductivity in Pd$_3$P$_2$(S$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_8$ Kagome-lattice compounds. These compounds exhibit a unique flat-band structure, and our study found that the superconducting transition temperature increases by 15% when pressurized from 120 to 150 GPa. Our analysis of the electronic structure and superconducting mechanism suggests that the emergence of stress-induced superconductivity in these compounds is linked to the presence of a flat band that facilitates the formation of unconventional superconducting pairs.

We demonstrate that black hole data can be recovered from information encoded in Wilson loops within topological JT gravity. Specifically, this data can be extracted from the boundary Ward identity, which expresses the variation of a Wilson loop's action with respect to bulk geometry. In the context of JT gravity, this identity relates variations in the asymptotic geometry's surface gravity to changes in the entanglement entropy gap, and by extension, can be used to reconstruct the surface gravity. Once the surface gravity is known, it becomes feasible to reconstruct the asymptotic geometry, albeit only up to an additive constant due to JT gravity's inherent ambiguity in the dilaton field.

Neural ODEs have proven to be highly effective for modeling time-dependent relationships in data, but their performance relies heavily on having continuous and error-free measurements. In contrast, real-world data often lacks this crucial assumption, featuring instead non-linear and unpredictable observations. Consequently, existing neural ODE methods may not always produce reliable results when dealing with noisy data. To address this issue, we introduce a neural ODE framework capable of handling and improving on data with high levels of noise. Specifically, we propose two novel methods. The first method, which we call neural ODE with unpredictable data, utilizes an approximation technique to account for errors in data by solving a minimax problem. The second method, which we call neural ODE with probabilistic data, uses a model-based approach to account for uncertainty in data by solving a set of optimization problems. Our experiments demonstrate that both methods outperform existing neural ODE methods in a variety of applications and we also show that they can be used in conjunction with one another to further enhance accuracy.

The Object Target Navigation challenge in robotics and AI requires navigating to a target object within a cluttered space. Current approaches primarily focus on either learning object and environment representations or generating policies directly from sensory data. However, these methods often struggle with object and environment changes, particularly when the target object is out of sight. To address this issue, we introduce the Object Recall Transformer, a novel method that utilizes the Transformer architecture to model object and environment representations. By leveraging this approach, OTNet is capable of recalling objects and remembering environmental features, thereby improving overall performance. In our experiments, OTNet outperforms current standards on a range of challenging navigation tasks, as well as showcases its robustness in complex, cluttered environments with moving objects.

Current methods for fine-tuning pre-trained language models with instructions have several drawbacks, including the need for manual selection and limited fine-tuning capacity. To address these issues, we developed OPT-IML, an effective and efficient approach that automatically selects suitable instructions for each task and enhances model fine-tuning capacity by 10 times. Our experiments on task-free instruction learning from pre-trained models using multiple instruction sources revealed that OPt-IML outperforms existing methods by a significant 6.7% absolute score on GLUE.

The engagement of peripheral users in collaborative software development projects is a complex phenomenon that can be difficult to analyze. This issue is particularly relevant in open-source communities, such as Scratch, where the diverse contributions of various users coexist and evolve over time. To understand these dynamics, we developed a new statistical framework to categorize and examine the behavior of active contributors in Scratch. Our findings, based on a 4-month analysis of the community, reveal distinct patterns of engagement among core and peripheral users, as well as a diverse range of peripheral roles. Furthermore, we observed that approximately half of all peripheral users engage in authentic contributions, and we identified specific characteristics associated with the peripheral roles. These results provide valuable insights for the development of effective strategies to engage external users in collaborative projects.

The static electronic properties of a homogeneous electron gas are investigated using a transcorrelated Hamiltonian, which accurately incorporates electron-electron correlation through a unitary transformation of the electronic Hamiltonian. Building on previous research, our study improves upon existing methods by employing a more robust basis near the Fermi surface, resulting in significantly reduced perturbation energies, down to an order of magnitude decrease compared to a standard basis. This increase in accuracy allows for more precise computation of electronic properties, such as the condensation energy and the electronic polarization and Kohn parameter, which are found to be in line with both transcorrelated calculations and existing density functional theory results.

We introduce a method to restrict covariance matrices in probabilistic slam based on physical constraints derived from position uncertainty. This approach is informed by the application of optimal transport theory. By applying the proposed restricted maximum likelihood estimation, the covariance matrix can be factorized into two separate matrices, one of which represents the localization uncertainty and the other the mapping uncertainty. This separation is beneficial for applications such as filtering and error calibration, as it allows localization uncertainty to be estimated using sensor models and mapping uncertainty to be controlled by a user parameter. This enhanced control enables the optimization of the reliability of the pose graph optimization solution to suit the requirements of the application.

The rapid growth of data in modern computing has led to numerous applications that heavily rely on large-scale data sharing.  However, ensuring data privacy in this process is a pressing challenge. A new safeguarding method for sensitive data is proposed in this paper, leveraging an innovative approach to tensor network decomposition and an efficient computation strategy for scattered tensors. This hybrid approach is called RTND-SCOT, and it offers a balance of efficiency and accuracy in data representation. Specifically, RTND-SCOT is capable of utilizing a large number of data samples to generate low-rank approximations while maintaining data privacy. Additionally, it can be combined with various data compression methods to facilitate data sharing. A thorough theoretical analysis of RTND-SCOT is provided, along with experimental results that demonstrate its superiority in data safeguarding over other tensor network decomposition techniques.

The integration of robots in human daily life is rapidly expanding, but their widespread adoption is hindered by the perception of uncertainty surrounding their safety. A potential solution lies in using simulation-to-real transfer, where a policy learned in simulation is directly applied to real-world robots. However, this method is often compromised by the risk of robot failure. This study proposes SafeAPT, a novel simulation-to-real transfer algorithm, designed to minimize the likelihood of unsafe robot behavior. By utilizing a set of pre-trained policies with varied parameters, SafeAPT can accurately predict the performance of the real robot, ensuring safe transfer. A specific example of SafeAPT involves using reinforcement learning to develop policies with different parameters, simulating their performance in a virtual environment, and then using the collected data to build a safety model. This model is then used to determine the parameters of the policies deemed safe for real-world robot transfer. Experiments using SafeAPT have demonstrated its effectiveness, resulting in a significant reduction in the risk of robot failure, with a notable decrease of 60% in the average cost of robot failure.

The presence of collimated outflows, or jets, is a common feature in various compact radio sources across different luminosity levels. Observations of these jets in the context of radio galaxies and quasars often exhibit distinct characteristics, such as twisted patterns, opening angles, and velocity distributions. This article aims to provide a concise overview of the prevailing views on jet formation and discuss their role in the evolution of active galactic nuclei. Furthermore, it touches on the unique characteristics observed in the broad- and narrow-line radio galaxies within the z~1 environment.

This research presents an innovative approach to analyzing nonstationary and nonlinear time series data, specifically focusing on regression applications. By combining concurrent sieve methods, the proposed framework addresses two significant issues: model nonstationarity and nonlinear dynamics under nonergodic conditions. Our method is validated through experimental evidence and theoretical convergence properties. This approach is applied to financial analysis, where the performance is evaluated using real-world datasets.

This study examines the challenges of identifying aggressive language and proposes a novel approach utilizing neural networks and pre-trained language models to enhance the accuracy of text-based classification. By developing a pipeline that leverages the BERT model to encode language, we evaluate the effectiveness of including contextual information derived from character-level inputs in binary classification tasks. Our analysis, which applies this pipeline to three aggressive language datasets, reveals that integrating contextual information from character-level inputs and selective word-level inputs respectively can improve the accuracy of binary classification tasks by 3.7% to 9.2%.

The brain's many parts interact in multiple ways, yet the connections and strengths between them remain unclear. To address this, researchers have used a data-driven approach that analyzes brain activity while a person performs tasks and identifies connections that become active. This method, called connectome dynamics, relies on assumptions about how brain regions interact, but these assumptions can be limiting. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a new approach that uses a type of artificial neural network to model how brain regions communicate without making any specific assumptions first. This new method, called data-informed connectivity, allows us to identify the strengths of connections based on how well it replicates brain activity patterns. We tested this method using data from a specific group of tasks and found that the connections we identified were consistent with what was previously found, even when we used only a small number of tasks. This new approach is useful because it doesn't require any specific assumptions about how brain regions communicate and can be used to identify connections that may not be present in existing data.

We have developed a time-optimized dissipative system that incorporates Nesterov's accelerated algorithm, yielding a stable vector of values. Our approach leverages the transformation of a dissipative system that lacks a fixed point, via a unique transformation, to produce a system with a stable fixed point that aligns with Nesterov's technique. Building upon this foundation, we have devised a dynamic system that mirrors the optimized time progression of Nesterov's algorithm, thereby creating a trajectory that converges to a vector of optimal values.

This study focuses on developing boundary treatments for implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods in hyperbolic systems with oscillating source terms, where high-accuracy time-stepping is achieved by combining high-order methods for the hyperbolic part and the Struve function for the forcing term. By implementing particle-flux-based methods at boundaries, where variables are treated as flux rather than state variables, high-order accuracy can be retained at boundary interfaces. Furthermore, we propose and evaluate two approaches to handle the forcing term at boundaries, which yield results that are comparable in efficiency and accuracy to recent numerical methods.

To increase the absorption of thin solar cells, a special mirror is used to reflect sunlight that would otherwise be lost. A numerical analysis was conducted to assess the impact of different back reflectors on the absorption of thin solar cells, focusing on various thicknesses, absorption coefficients, and mirror designs. The study compared the performance of different back reflectors, including metal, dielectric, and photonic band gap structures, and found that these structures can significantly enhance absorption, particularly in thin solar cells, with absorption rates of 90% achievable in some cases. The study also identified the optimal conditions for the different back reflectors and their limitations.

In cases where machine learning algorithms are deployed in high-stakes environments, uncertainty about model parameters or data distribution may arise due to unforeseen circumstances. To mitigate these issues, we present a method for combining Bayesian and Dempster-Shafer reasoning in inferential networks. This approach enables the generation of a credibility distribution for a target variable based on the given data, incorporating both Bayesian uncertainty and missing information. Theoretical foundations of this method are established, and two case studies are provided to illustrate its practical application.

The task of K-suggestion is a well-studied problem in the context of web search and content recommendation, where users seek the most relevant content based on their search query. One widely used approach involves mapping user queries to a vector space where the suggestion is selected from the top-K most similar vectors. However, traditional methods for learning this mapping rely on a fixed margin between relevant and irrelevant vectors, which can lead to suboptimal results. In this paper, a probabilistic K-suggestion method is proposed that dynamically adjusts the margin between relevant and irrelevant vectors during training. Theoretical analysis of this model reveals that the proposed method minimizes an upper bound on the expected loss and thus offers better performance. The results of experiments on several real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this model, with significant improvements over traditional methods.

Theorized in 2008, quantum Markovianity has been rigorously defined for open systems in 2010, yet its application to specific types of open systems is limited due to difficulties in some system or environment scenarios. In 2017, a generalized concept of non-Markovianity was developed, applicable to various quantum systems, including those that are non-orthodox. This paper examines and confirms the long-term non-Markovianity in a generalized type of quantum system, with a focus on a specific instance where the memory of this system fails to be erased.

To achieve reliable artificial intelligence, particularly in high-risk situations such as healthcare, self-explaining AI is essential. In an effort to address this requirement, this study presents a novel, non-inferential approach to artificial intelligence called Counterfactual Learning, which combines engaged learning and counterfactual inference. The Counterfactual Inference module, built on the Counterfactual Baseline model, offers self-explaining capabilities by generating human-intelligible explanations for classification results, enabling users to make more informed decisions. The Engaged Learning module, designed to enhance model interpretability, encourages users to ask more relevant questions and refines the model accordingly. Our proposed Counterfactual Baseline outperforms the baseline model, yielding a significant 10% improvement in F1-Score when classifying PPI network protein-ligand binding affinity scores. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of our proposed framework in generating counterfactual explanations and the benefits of engaged learning for model interpretability.

To evaluate the effectiveness of a semantic mapping system, a virtual environment with a simulated robot that navigates and interacts with its surroundings would be ideal. This allows researchers to experiment with various techniques without the challenges of working with real robots and environments, such as limited access to physical robots and inconsistent natural environments. We introduce RoSmEEry, a simulation platform that generates realistic environments and robot paths, which can be used to benchmark semantic mapping systems. The platform offers a range of tools to create a wide variety of scenes and situations.

Rikudo is a Japanese board game with a strategic element, first introduced in 2018. It's a six-player game aiming to claim victory by accumulating 11 points. Players achieve points through various methods, including forming combinations of tiles that meet specific group and sequence requirements. If a player's combination does not meet these criteria, it remains on the board, potentially enabling other players to build upon it and use its components for their own combinations. It was initially assumed that determining the best move in Rikudo is a computationally manageable task. Contrary to this assumption, a recent study has proven that Rikudo is an NP-complete game, indicating that determining the best move in Rikudo is a computationally difficult task, effectively rendering it unsolvable by conventional methods, especially for large games with numerous tiles.

High-capacity transport systems, encompassing vast networks and cloud computing, are crucial for today's complex systems. These systems are characterized by immense scales, intricate structures, and diverse decision-making processes. As a result, they pose significant computational challenges when attempting to find the most efficient transport strategies. In this paper, we introduce a framework for examining the challenges of computing optimal transport values and propose two numerical techniques to address these issues. We provide a comprehensive analysis of the properties of the cost function and the optimal transport map. Furthermore, we use these insights to compare the convergence rates of the two proposed methods. To validate our approach, we apply the optimal transport framework to multiple scenarios of high-capacity transportation, including single-level and multi-level networks, cloud computing, and high-capacity transport with preferences.

Ramanujan's work on his modular form 1-72^2+72^2 has been further explored and generalized, with relationships to Hecke transformations and self-inverses of Hecke polynomials established, resulting in new results including a Ramanujan-Petersson-like congruence involving the series in question and Euler's polynomials, as well as generalized versions of Albert Inoue's modular equations and a set of modular relations to the Cohen-Kimberling cubic recurrence.

We have obtained high-resolution spectra of eight lensed quasars, each of which exhibits a strong quasar emission line, and a distinct image with a clear central gap, and in all cases, the spectra of the lensing galaxies were successfully isolated. We have made precise measurements of the redshifts and velocity dispersions of the lensing galaxies, and found these to be in good agreement with predictions based on simple strong lensing models, thereby confirming the accuracy of the predictions and enabling the measurement of the effect of the gravitational potential on the quasar's line profiles.

This study introduces and analyzes the solution to a q-Alembert nonlinear fractional differential equation. By employing the Banach fixed point principle after modifying the equation's variance, the existence and uniqueness of the solution is proven. Subsequent numerical examples are provided to validate the obtained results.

The phonon Hall effect is a direct result of breaking time-reversal symmetry within
harmonic crystals through strain. To analyze this phenomenon, we utilize an extension of
Berry curvature's definition, applicable to Riemannian manifolds. Our approach reveals a
geometric link between the phonon Hall effect and the anholonomy of crystal lattice
vectors, an inherent property that also enables us to calculate Berry curvature
through curved crystal band structures.

This article provides matrix extensions of the Fejér and Levin-Stel'kin inequalities for analytic functions. Specifically, it formulates matrix versions of these inequalities with respect to the norms of the Hardy space H2, as well as with respect to the Bessel and Toeplitz operator scales. The key to deriving these inequalities involves establishing a matrix version of the mean ergodic theorem on the Hardy space H2.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for the spacetime resulting from the evaporation of a black hole, as initially proposed by Page. Our findings indicate that beyond a specific point, no matter how early in a light-travel time from the black hole, the mean null energy condition will be violated on the horizon. Notably, this contradicts Page's initial assumption that the null energy condition holds at late times. Instead, we discover that if the mean null energy condition holds at some point before the black hole fully evaporates, it will also hold for the remainder of the evaporation process.

This research examines the fundamental characteristics of conformal field theories (CFTs) that are compact and have no defects, with a focus on their shared underlying structure. It demonstrates how various CFT traits are interconnected within a modular framework. A novel CFT structure framework is presented, which categorizes all CFTs by their compact symmetry characteristics. This framework allows for a systematic approach to classifying and studying CFTs. A new, automated classification system is proposed, based on the existing classification system, which groups CFTs by their 2D field theory structure. Additionally, the text covers the essential concepts of CFT, including the principles of operator algebras, state sum invariants, and the modular group, and discusses their applications in CFT classification and their connections to other theories. It also explores the interconnections between different CFT concepts, such as the relationship between the 2D and 3D dualities, and the implications of the modular group for the Poincar\'e-Hitchin series.

Industrial control systems have become increasingly integrated with the internet, making them more susceptible to cyber threats that can disrupt critical public services. Despite the growing risks, there remains a shortage of reliable information systems to evaluate the robustness of ICS security. In response, we've developed a unique Cybersecurity Evaluation Framework Maturity Model, referred to as the ICS-CTM2 model, which assesses an organization's ability to manage cybersecurity within their ICS infrastructure. This framework is based on the Conceptual Framework of Cybersecurity (CF-CW), which categorizes cybersecurity as a social, technical, and organizational issue. By using the ICS-CTM2 framework, organizations can establish a comprehensive approach to address cybersecurity challenges, including implementing new cybersecurity systems and strategies. This will enable them to effectively mitigate existing risks and develop a comprehensive cybersecurity plan.

In the context of Reinforcement Learning, a new approach, Avarice-driven Value Depiction, or ADVD, is introduced to enhance cooperation among multiple agents. ADVD achieves this by allowing agents to share information through value sharing and its updated policy network uses this shared information to inform decisions. ADVD's value depiction method ensures that its values accurately represent the collaborative interests of all agents. Through a loss function based on a model's self-interest, the value depiction's accuracy is measured. ADVD's unique design allows for the creation of collaborative games where individual and collaborative rewards coexist, which is beneficial for modeling real-world interactions. ADVD's effectiveness was demonstrated in scenarios requiring cooperation among multiple agents.

Recent studies have found that language models can perpetuate harmful biases against various groups, including women, minorities, and the elderly. This work investigates how these models have internalized stereotypes about long-standing social groups: older adults, the working class, and women. To investigate this, we've developed StereoSet, a new corpus with tasks designed to assess stereotypical bias in language models. Using StereoSet, we've evaluated a range of frameworks, including two neural models and two embedded models, across 42 tasks. Our analysis reveals that all tested models have significant biases against working-class and elderly individuals. Furthermore, we've discovered that models often use phrases like "is very old" to predict age-based characteristics, rather than relying on age-specific traits. Our research also identified that removing biases from language models can be a complex process, as it may involve trade-offs that affect model performance.

This study introduces an off-policy reinforcement learning technique to improve
distant speech enhancement, focusing on the electrical tilt parameter in a
continuous speech processing context. The challenge of controlling this parameter
is explored, where traditional methods rely on discrete tilt settings limited by
model capabilities. An off-policy learning approach utilizing a deep neural network
model is proposed, enabling continuous control of the electrical tilt parameter.
The approach involves a bootstrapping objective and accounts for unobserved
actions during training. Experimental results on the WSJ corpus reveal that the
proposed method outperforms baseline electrical tilt values and achieves the best
word error rate (5.68%) compared to state-of-the-art speech enhancement models.

The LHCb collaboration has provided multiple estimates of the CKM angle $\gamma$ based on data from Run 1, with the results showing global compatibility with the CKM unitarity constraints. This article introduces a new method that enables combining these individual likelihoods into a single, more informative estimate of $\gamma$ with a corresponding uncertainty. This technique relies on a single parameterization of the unitarity triangle and can easily accommodate future $\gamma$ estimates from LHCb, as well as potential multi-system likelihoods from other experiments.

This research paper delves into the intricate properties of a family of complex ellipsoids. These ellipsoids are three-dimensional projections of a family of two-dimensional ellipses within a four-dimensional space. The symmetrical structure of the ellipsoids can be represented by vectors with a specific relationship, where vectors sum up to a total magnitude of 2. The study of these ellipsoids leads to the identification of several fundamental questions. The paper demonstrates the existence of these ellipsoids, providing a method for their construction. The authors also introduce a concept of equivalence among the various complex ellipsoids. The study ultimately uncovers an intriguing property, demonstrating that any two distinct, inequivalent complex ellipsoids can be used to generate a three-dimensional space containing an integral lattice structure without a line. The paper contributes to a broader research initiative by hypersurfaces, offering a contribution to a family of related projects.

People are increasingly concerned about their personal data, but existing methods for sharing this information, such as social networking sites, are lacking in essential controls and may prioritize profit over user well-being. A more organized, user-friendly approach to data marketplaces is proposed as a more appealing alternative, but little is known about how users respond to these platforms' controls and functionalities. Our study involved conducting in-depth interviews with 29 individuals to assess their willingness to engage with a data marketplace, and the results indicate that they appreciate market-based pricing structures, prefer to manage their personal data themselves, and appreciate clear and understandable terms of use. Users also expect higher compensation for their data and prefer to manage their personal information selectively. Our findings suggest that developing a user-friendly data marketplace requires prioritizing user control, providing detailed information about data usage, and implementing data segmentation to accommodate various user needs.

In 5G uplink systems utilizing non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), base stations receive and process superimposed signals from multiple users with varying quality, including both high and low signal-to-noise ratios. This complexity increases with non-orthogonal signaling, particularly with non-uniformly spaced symbols that are more challenging to decode. List sphere decoding (LSD) has been proposed as a solution, but its efficiency decreases with an increase in symbols spacing. This paper presents a deep learning-driven LSD framework, aimed at resolving NOMA recognition issues, particularly with non-uniformly spaced symbols. The proposed approach is designed to handle the recognition of superimposed symbols with any degree of non-uniform spacing. The LSD process is formulated as a problem of finding the closest symbol in a predefined list to a given signal, which is formulated as a problem of finding the minimum Euclidean distance. Inspired by the minimum distance-based problem, a neural network is trained to learn the relationship between symbols and signals. The trained network is then used to generate a set of symbols, serving as a list for LSD. Simulation results show that the proposed deep learning-driven LSD outperforms traditional LSD by achieving a 2.5 dB gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in recognizing FTN signals with randomly spaced symbols.

Impact algebras serve as a simplified model of finite-dimensional Hilbert space topology. This study establishes the Topological Arrangement and Frink Ideal Hierarchy on the set of all proper impact algebras and subsequently demonstrates that these topological sequences converge. The work also identifies and categorizes specific topological characteristics on the set of all pre-impact algebras and pre-Deegre algebras.

Deep neural networks are particularly adept at recognizing common, representative patterns in their training data, often overlooking the diverse and unconventional examples that can significantly improve their performance on unfamiliar scenarios. This limitation is addressed through a novel approach known as SaliencyMix, which incorporates random, secondary image elements in an adaptive manner to enhance model robustness. By identifying the regions most critical for accurate classification, SaliencyMix selectively embeds minor objects into these areas, thereby preventing overfitting and improving the model's ability to generalize. Experimental evaluations on numerous datasets have consistently shown that SaliencyMix outperforms existing regularization techniques, demonstrating the method's general applicability to various data augmentation strategies.

We investigate the properties of modules over the infinite-dimensional Iwahari-Hecke ring $\Hinf$, focusing on modules with trace maps drawn from the same ring. It's established that any such module with a non-trivial trace map, under certain conditions, must be the equivalent of a simple $\Hinf$-module. Conversely, for any finite-dimensional $\Hinf$-module, we demonstrate that its trace map can be derived as a homomorphism to $\Hinf$. Additionally, for any $\Hinf$-module with a finite and non-zero trace map, we prove it must be isomorphic to a module constructed from a semisimple finite-dimensional $\Hinf$-module.

A novel method is proposed utilizing the combined effect of intrinsic galaxy alignments and cosmic shear on galaxy ellipticity to serve as an additional tool to evaluate the gravitational theories beyond $\Lambda$CDM. The proposed method is based on the concept that the intrinsic galaxy shapes and the cosmic shear on galaxies are independent, which allows the method to be sensitive to modified gravity. The effectiveness of this method is tested using the semi-analytical model HALO-ENZO simulation and is found to be competitive with the shear-only method. The proposed method is also less susceptible to contamination from non-Halo terms and can be used in conjunction with the shear-only method. The intrinsic alignments method is also found to be less affected by the non-simultaneity of the galaxy sampling in different redshifts.

Our research examines the dynamic interactions of dense, soft-matter systems composed of spheres that can change shape, and with varying mechanical stiffness. Through the use of computer simulations, we investigate the effects of particle stiffness on static and dynamic properties in these systems, particularly their responses to steady shear flow at low shear rates. We find that the systems composed of soft particles exhibit unique rheological properties when compared to systems of elastic particles. Notably, the systems of soft particles demonstrate an increase in shear stress that is directly proportional to the square of shear rate, and a viscosity that is directly proportional to the square of volume fraction, characteristic of frictionally interacting materials. However, the systems of soft particles also exhibit properties that are distinct from those of elastic particles, including a non-zero shear stress at low shear rates, and a non-linear relationship between viscosity and volume fraction. These findings are in agreement with experimental observations of granular materials such as sand and coal, and suggest that the effects of particle deformability play a significant role in the dynamics of real granular materials under low shear rates.

A data-driven approach has been developed to model and analyze the diffusion of gold nanoparticles through cell membranes over time, considering various factors such as size, charge, and lipidity. This method combines a simulation of these processes in free space and within the cell membrane with a process to integrate experimental data, and is applied using data from in vitro cell lines. The model effectively captures how particle size impacts diffusion, and also demonstrates the importance of particle charge in influencing fusion rates, revealing a critical threshold below which particles fail to fuse.

This study introduces parameterized division theorems and bifurcations for operators associated with infinite-dimensional linearized elasticity and plate theory kernels, which have a Laplace domain that's bounded on the left side by the imaginary axis. The research develops an abstract theory of parameterized division theorems that can be applied to operators with Fredholm interposition, which in turn enables parameterized bifurcation analysis of operators with such kernels. The theory is developed in an abstract setting and later applied to specific types of operators related to infinite-dimensional elastic systems.

The concept of taste tastes, although subjective and often conflicting, can be objectively evaluated in a laboratory setting through chemical means. Research has shown that taste perception responds to specific chemical characteristics and its regulation is controlled by precise mechanisms. As a result, we believe the fundamental characteristics of taste should be based on objective, physicochemically measurable factors. This paper presents a three-part framework for understanding taste, consisting of the governing principles, the essential elements, and the fundamental rules. The key components of this framework are organized into a tetrahedron structure, demonstrating how the fundamental concepts of taste are interconnected and governed by a unified principle of specific chemical interactions.

This paper introduces for the first time novel identities for $(h;q)$-Genocchi values and polynomials in an infinite series of numbers, which can be considered as an extension of the well-known Genocchi numbers. Additionally, the study leverages the weight beta function to develop new identities involving $(h;q)$-Genocchi polynomials. It also utilizes the $(h;q)$-Genocchi polynomials to derive Fermi--Carlitz polynomials, which in turn leads to the derivation of an extension of the Watt's (a; b)-Duranov polynomials. Finally, the present research provides various consequences of the developed identities.

To address the growing need for universal healthcare, it's essential to improve therapy delivery through automation. However, this automation effort is hindered by the complexity of predicting long-term patient outcomes, which has been a significant challenge for healthcare providers. To address this issue, we propose a novel reinforcement learning method that simulates human decision-making processes. This approach utilizes a cognitive architecture that mimics human behavior when making therapy decisions, ultimately enabling the creation of a virtual human agent capable of making therapy decisions. Our model is then trained using the Dynamic Brain-Inspired Reinforcement Learning (DBIRL) algorithm, which incorporates dynamic neural network parameters to simulate human decision-making variability. The proposed model is then validated using the Alzheimer's Dementia Therapy simulation, and the results indicate that the DBIRL outperforms other algorithms, achieving a higher overall reward score.

In epidemiological and case-control studies, individuals' memory biases distort recall, particularly in the initial few months following an exposure or event. We propose a causal inference framework to address memory distortion, allowing the derivation of two key correlation concepts: the exposure-recall relationship and the incidence-distribution relationship. The former indicates that exposure can influence how events are remembered, while the latter shows that the distribution of event experiences can affect how events are recalled. We also outline methods to account for the distortion in case-control studies, focusing on the exposure-recall relationship. Our approach is illustrated using US military veterans' data related to Influenza-like illness risk, and the findings suggest that the perceived association between exposure and disease may be an illusion.

Generative models can be categorized into two groups: invertible models that use reversible maps and non-invertible models that use parameterized generative networks. The invertible models offer precise likelihood calculations, whereas non-invertible models are limited by intractable log determinant log terms. A novel approach is proposed by combining invertible and non-invertible techniques, resulting in efficient likelihood computations without sacrificing distribution approximations. Specifically, the method involves incorporating invertible layers within the network's feed-forward structure to enable precise likelihood calculations without inverting the entire network. Furthermore, the theoretical foundations of this approach are explored, and experiments demonstrate its efficacy on both synthetic and real-world data.

In today's data-driven society, cities generate vast amounts of information from diverse sources, which can inform numerous projects and initiatives. Effective management of these data points is crucial for governance and development in urban settings. The application of machine learning and data visualization techniques has the potential to unlock the full potential of urban data. Our research aims to evaluate the impact of feature correlations in machine learning model predictions by analyzing a range of related factors. Through our findings, we seek to identify key urban data features that can inform city development and growth. The outcomes of our study can be applied in assessing proposed projects and evaluating their potential impact on cities.

This research explores the HDG-P0 method for reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes problems, creating optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners and verifying their effectiveness through theoretical and numerical evidence. The study establishes that the HDG-P0 method generates matrices with a condition number of O(h^{-2}) for the reaction-diffusion equation and O(h^{-3/2}) for the generalized Stokes problem. Correspondingly, the optimal coercive multigrid preconditioners condition numbers are O(h^{-2}) and O(h^{-3/2}) respectively. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings and demonstrate the multigrid preconditioner's effectiveness.

The standard statistical measure, often expressed as a likelihood ratio, can be limited when data is missing and can lead to misleading conclusions when available data is limited. In contrast, sensitivity measures in diagnostic testing provide a more interpretable concept in such situations. This is because they consider the prevalence of conditions and test characteristics. To address this issue, we have developed a Bayesian framework that incorporates uncertainty and evaluates the impact of missing data. This new statistical measure is based on the E-value, recently introduced as a sensitivity measure for diagnostic tests, and is calculated using posterior predictive sampling. Our proposed method is applied to evaluate the impact of missing data on the association between vitamin D levels and certain autoimmune disorders, demonstrating the proposed approach's utility in assessing the reliability of observational studies affected by data loss due to missingness.

A novel statistical approach, the Crossover Residual Variance Test, is developed for analyzing complex crossover designs that often encounter missing data due to limitations in conducting experiments on all test subjects. This approach calculates critical probabilities based on Cochran's variance ratio test to determine significant crossover effects, allowing it to identify missing data patterns that impact its accuracy. Simulation-based evaluations of various designs confirm the method's reliability, particularly when data is missing completely at random. This approach is also applied to analyze the efficacy of a novel oral bisoprolol formulation versus a time-matched placebo in a clinical trial.

A category with specific properties, such as being related to Cohen-Macaulay complexes and certain types of convex polytopes, is called a $K$-preadietary category. This category is a framework that can help analyze relationships between the properties of certain mathematical objects called associahedra. We will explore this framework further, examining its properties, particularly a key pairing between the directions of these objects, known as the "macronomial coexponential product." Our work builds on existing theories of other frameworks, such as Koszul categories, to generalize and extend these concepts.

DRAM manufacturers have adopted the monolithic memory organization, where multiple memory chips are integrated on a single die, to increase yields and minimize waste. This setup allows memory capacities to scale while keeping production costs low. Modern systems, including high-performance and high-speed systems, are designed to accommodate large arrays of memory, however, this comes at the cost of limited access and reduced programmability. To overcome these limitations and allow for more customizable memory systems, we propose the concept of CODIC - a memory substrate that enables the integration of new memory capabilities. CODIC achieves this by utilizing the existing interconnects within DRAM chips and introducing a new memory interface that allows for more flexible access patterns. This is complemented by a software framework that allocates and manages memory access for applications, ensuring efficient use of available memory resources. CODIC is designed to be compatible with standard DRAM technology, making it suitable for use with existing memory capacities.

This research paper delves into the use of functional programming in designing and modeling complex network systems, with a focus on the properties that allow it to effectively manage and control network resources. Building on previous research (Part I) which explored its application in the management and orchestration of network resources, Part II presents a new software architecture that utilizes functional programming in the design and modeling of virtualized networks. The proposed architecture enables the efficient management of large-scale networks, offering a range of benefits including improved network asset management, scalability, high portability, modularity, modifiableness, and reusable code. To demonstrate its practical application, we present a real-world example of virtualized network systems, including a virtualized network system with multiple interconnected networks, as well as a network asset management system that utilizes functional programming to effectively manage and model complex networks.

Implementing fault-tolerant quantum operations is crucial for advancing large-scale quantum computing initiatives. To assess the feasibility of operations for specific applications, their resource requirements can be analyzed. This study investigates the energy costs associated with executing single-qubit operations and multi-qubit operations on the toric code, utilizing the toric code's native encoding scheme. The research reveals higher energy costs for multi-qubit operations, specifically a 2dB increase compared to single-qubit operations, primarily due to the need for additional auxiliary qubits. To investigate the resources needed for specific gate types, this study examines the performance of the toric code under various conditions, including different types of measurement errors and the impact of finite transverse field shifts. The analysis indicates that, to achieve a high fidelity of 0.995, a resource cost of approximately 1.35 is required.

A comprehensive overview is provided of the initial planning phase and developed capabilities of the OPUS job management system, which was designed for the European Southern Observatory's proposed Virtual Observatory project, General Director's Initiative for Astrophysics and Astronomy. To achieve the desired flexibility, scalability, and interoperability, particularly in conjunction with the European Southern Observatory's service registry, a service-oriented architecture was chosen for the OPUS system, incorporating peer-to-peer execution and registry registration. This system adheres to established VO standards, including WS-Peer, WSRF, and GMPL, to create a seamless and efficient framework. To streamline the submission process, the initial version of the OPUS Web Service client was developed using Python and the PyWSDL library, allowing for the creation of a WSDL file. This service enables the submission of job requests via a Web interface or command-line utility. This paper presents the underlying architecture, capabilities, and initial results of the OPUS system.

Incorporating interactivity, rather than passive learning, is a highly effective approach for educational content development, particularly when it comes to complex topics like wireless networks. Notably, digital game-based learning has been shown to be an ideal method for enhancing the learning experience. However, the majority of existing studies have focused on practical applications rather than the educational aspects. To address this knowledge gap, this research proposes an innovative interactive learning approach that leverages wireless sensor technology to teach intricate wireless network concepts. By providing hands-on training, the learning method equips students with the necessary practical skills and hands-on experience for network applications. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, the research will employ both quantitative and qualitative evaluation methods, including surveys, interviews, and technical assessments. Notably, the preliminary results indicate that the learning materials developed using this approach significantly enhance students' understanding of wireless networks and their ability to apply learning principles in real-world scenarios.

The widely accepted relationship between ozone and molecular oxygen has been questioned by certain studies, which have suggested that both gases might be generated by photochemical processes that do not depend on the initial O2 abundance. In order to assess the validity of the O2-O3 correlation on exoplanets, we have reevaluated this relationship through photochemical simulations of Earth-like atmospheres containing N2, CO2, CH4, O2, and CH4, with H2O also considered as an intermediate in the O2 production pathway. The simulations revealed that the O2-O3 correlation is robust, stable, and consistent across different models, with O3 concentrations varying linearly in response to changes in O2 abundance. The results of these simulations are in agreement with observations of several terrestrial planets and moons, as well as with theoretical models of non-hydrocarbon atmospheres. The O2-O3 correlation is also expected to remain consistent on Earth even if future climate scenarios involve significant CO2 reductions, with O2 being completely depleted in the atmosphere, and CH4 being replaced by increasing concentrations of N2.

In non-equilibrium steady states within the Hofstadter model, an unusual quantum fluid behavior emerges at the surface where particles exhibit counter-intuitive properties similar to the polariton bound states that form in coupled light-matter systems. These bound states are unique in that they are resistant to perturbations, a trait that is maintained even when the Hofstadter Hamiltonian is altered significantly, as long as the underlying topological structure remains intact. The existence of these robust states has important implications for the field of surface science.

Recent advancements in multilingual neural machine translation (NMT) have made it feasible to translate text across multiple languages. Nevertheless, even when a model has been trained on a particular set of languages, inaccuracies can still occur when translating words or phrases that are unique to those languages. Moreover, in medical contexts, this can result in the mistranslation of vital information. To mitigate these issues, we have developed a novel technique involving the utilization of specialized medical terminology dictionaries to fine-tune an existing NMT model, aiming to enhance translation accuracy and preserve clinical significance.

A theoretical model has been developed to describe the behavior of distinct types of solitary and shock waves within a multi-ion plasma system containing ions and electrons. This plasma system is characterized by a scheme where a background population of positive ions is modulated by a smaller population of positive electrons. This setup is necessary to produce the specified wave types. Analyzing a function of the electrons that is proportional to their fluid temperature allows for a simplified approach, enabling the investigation of the impact of electron fluid temperature variation on the properties of the waves. Modified-ion-acoustic solitary waves are produced under certain conditions, while shock waves are generated when the ion fluid temperature exceeds a critical value, resulting in a finite phase velocity. This phenomenon is supported by laboratory experiments and plasma devices.

Recent advancements in multi-lingual information retrieval have seen significant improvements through pretraining sentence representations using contrastive learning techniques. However, these advancements primarily focus on generating context-free representations. This study proposes an unsupervised approach for training context-sensitive sentence representations across multiple languages, leveraging the dense retrieval framework. By incorporating sentence representations into the embedding space, the model is able to learn a more language-invariant distribution of vectors. Experimental results from both English and French datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this pretraining method, achieving notable gains over the baseline, particularly in cases with limited training data.

Multimodal learning's effectiveness heavily relies on a crucial concept: selecting and prioritizing relevant modalities. Current approaches typically choose specific modalities for different tasks or inputs, but these approaches are often hindered by two main limitations. Firstly, they're restricted to using pre-determined modalities for input representation, which can be overly restrictive and neglect the potential of combining multiple modalities. Secondly, they're unable to dynamically adjust the modalities based on the task or input, which can lead to underutilization of available information. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel method called Prototypical Modal Adjustment (PMA), which learns to select relevant modalities by analyzing prototypical examples from each modality. PMA is capable of dynamically adjusting the modalities based on the task or input, as well as leveraging the unique strengths of each modality to improve overall performance. Furthermore, PMA can be seamlessly integrated with existing methods to enhance their performance. Through a series of experiments across multiple datasets, we demonstrate that PMA not only surpasses existing methods but also excels in various scenarios, including low-resource and zero-shot learning environments.

The interaction between a moving object and a surface, as observed in various transport phenomena, is investigated through the lens of conveyance theory. This theoretical framework, initially developed by Bocquet and Maisonneuve in 1993, posits that the friction coefficient depends on a single parameter, a dimensionless combination of viscosity and surface roughness, as well as the temperature. This study revisits the theory by incorporating vector calculations and surface topography into the analysis. By examining the dynamic interaction between a small object and a surface, the authors derive a general expression for the friction coefficient. Their findings suggest that the classical conveyance coefficient is a specific instance of a more comprehensive invariant, obtained by summing the components of a matrix related to the surface's topographical features. This formulation is expected to expand the theoretical framework, enabling the prediction of diverse conveyance behaviors associated with different surface topographies.

This study presents an innovative method for incorporating semantic information into a deep neural network-based acoustic model, specifically designed to handle speech commands within noisy environments. The proposed approach combines a deep neural network with a semi-parametric HMM, where the former handles speech feature extraction and the latter accounts for label-dependent factors. The standard variational approximation technique used in this paper allows for more efficient inference processes. Furthermore, our model employs a tensor decomposition method known as tensor-train, which significantly reduces the model's parameter count and memory requirements. The results of our experiments indicate that the proposed semi-supervised tensor-train model outperforms conventional ACNN models by achieving lower error rates, even when subjected to various levels of noise.

A new approach to calculate the dynamic behavior of two-level systems that interact with an external environment is presented, where the system interacts with multiple types of noise. This approach involves breaking down a complex master equation into smaller parts that can be more easily solved, and it accurately describes how the system evolves over time. This method has the advantage of being able to accurately describe rare events, and it allows for the creation of more realistic models of systems that are difficult to model with traditional methods. This approach is demonstrated by applying it to various types of noise and different initial conditions, and it reveals new insights into how the system behaves in certain situations.

We demonstrate through theoretical analysis that incorporating a thin-film silicon solar cell layer with silver and aluminum nanoparticles, arranged in a double-layered structure, can significantly enhance the solar cell's absorption capabilities. By examining the effects of varying nanoparticle size and concentration, we determine the optimal dimensions necessary to achieve the greatest absorption enhancement. Notably, we find that aluminum nanoparticles outperform their silver counterparts, resulting in a 94.24% increase in absorption efficiency when the concentration of aluminum nanoparticles is optimized at 2.5 x 10^13 cm^-3.

We are investigating the computational complexity of querying databases that contain only two values, yes or no, with operations such as union, intersection, and addition allowed. It is possible to solve any computation that can be done in polynomial time on a standard database model within this same time frame on the binary database model. However, when we limit the operations to only union, intersection, and subtraction, we find that certain computations, like counting, cannot be exactly replicated but some of them can still be done in polynomial time. Interestingly, we find that while some of the computations that can be done in polynomial time on the standard model cannot be done on the binary model, all of the standard model's computations that can be done in polynomial time can be done on the binary model when we include a selection operation in addition to union, intersection, and subtraction.

In recent years, researchers have increasingly utilized deep learning to develop video recognition models that can learn temporal and spatial patterns in video data. However, deep learning models typically necessitate a substantial amount of memory and computational resources, particularly when dealing with large datasets. To address this challenge, we propose a co-design strategy for combining algorithmic and hardware improvements to optimize the performance of Long Short-Term Memory networks for video identification tasks. Our approach involves decomposing deep learning models into lower-dimensional tensors using the Hierarchical Tucker decomposition technique, which enables efficient model compression and facilitates hardware acceleration. We also present a novel hardware accelerator design that incorporates Hierarchical Tucker decomposition and a high-throughput memory system to achieve high performance and energy efficiency. Experimental results using the large-scale YouTube dataset reveal that our approach can significantly reduce model size while maintaining a significant accuracy compared to state-of-the-art video recognition models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our proposed hardware architecture outperforms other tensor-based accelerators by delivering higher accuracy and energy efficiency in video identification tasks.

The MAVLink protocol, used by widely accepted open-source UAV software such as Ardupilot and PX4, lacks security measures, leaving it vulnerable to manipulation. Since the MAVLink protocol lacks authentication, an attacker can potentially gain control of UAVs using spoofed or manipulated MAVLink messages. To address this, research introduces MAVSec, a proposed protocol to safeguard the MAVLink communication. MAVSec incorporates a secure key exchange mechanism based on the Diffie-Hellman protocol, ensuring the authenticity of command messages and protecting against system-level vulnerabilities. It achieves this by encrypting command messages and verifying them using a public key-based signature verification system, also utilizing a one-time authentication token. The proposed solution was successfully implemented and tested within the Ardupilot framework, demonstrating its effectiveness in safeguarding UAVs from potential threats.

The concept of $N$ parallel processes communicating with one another to simulate the movement of particles in space is a complex task that becomes even more challenging when dealing with non-linear interactions. We have developed a new tool, Kollaps, designed to handle distributed dynamic graphs efficiently. This tool is unique in its ability to process graphs in real-time, adapting to changes and new data in a efficient and parallelized manner. Unlike traditional approaches that require pre-processing and fixed structures, Kollaps can handle a wide range of scenarios, including the collapse of a star cluster into a spherical shape, a process that cannot be simulated using traditional methods. We have successfully demonstrated the capabilities of Kollaps through its application in two complex scenarios: the collapse of a star cluster and the expansion of a fractal tree.

By exploring the underlying structure of twistor spaces, we uncover a clear connection between their structure and the generalized eigenfunction decomposition of complex line bundles, also revealing a natural correspondence to the Newman-Penrose formalism, providing an alternative basis for understanding space-time properties through twistor methods.

The Muon Detector, situated within the MAST-C detector at the Boulby Deep Underground Laboratory in the United Kingdom, is designed to capture cosmic ray muons. This detector aims to create a detailed underground map using the muon radiography technique, which can determine the local composition of the earth's composition. A novel, sensitive muon detector with a target location of 210 meters below ground will be developed to achieve high spatial resolution and precise event reconstruction, allowing researchers to create an accurate 3D map of the surrounding earth's composition. This research focuses on designing an active surface plate for the MAST-C detector and developing a readout system for the 204-pixel SiPM matrix.

Non-standard arithmetic operations are typically evaluated from left to right, similar to simple calculations. Recently developed languages such as Calco and Xrational rely on what is called a graph left left (GLL) semantics, where expressions are evaluated from right to left. It has been suggested that understanding the behavior of GLL requires developing a distinct model of how expressions are evaluated. This paper aims to test this hypothesis by formally defining a GLL calculus and demonstrating that it accurately models Calco's behavior on lists.

This research investigates the phenomenon of vacuum Cherenkov radiation in a $U(1)$ gauge theory, specifically at high temperatures, with an emphasis on how it relates to the electroweak phase transition. The study assumes that the Standard Model's Higgs field behaves similarly to a fermion with a small mass gap, and considers the impact of both zero and non-zero temperature on the process. It also explores the potential connection to the Standard Model's phase transition by calculating the relativistic relaxation time associated with the process and comparing it to the rate of the phase transition. The analysis employs a framework based on the Bethe-Salpeter equation and the Furry picture, and involves a numerical evaluation of the associated vertex function.

This study examines the relationship between people's perception of probability and their verbal predictions of future events, focusing on how these predictions vary across individuals. A novel approach is proposed, leveraging neural language models to provide a quantitative measure of each participant's verbal predictions, which are compared against the subjective probability estimates reported by each participant. The analysis reveals a notable gap between the verbal and subjective assessments of probability. To address the issue of evaluating these verbal predictions, a new approach is developed, which takes into account both the verbal prediction itself and the context within which it was made. The results show that this method is effective in capturing the variations in verbal predictions among individuals.

A new approach to determining the three-dimensional position of an object in a scene is presented, which utilizes the object's rotation to infer position. The approach, referred to as unintentional turntables, is applicable to both moving and stationary cameras. Initially, it is challenging to acquire sufficient negative samples, resulting from the necessity of a large number of views of the object from various positions. To address this issue, a method is developed to automatically select positive views and create positive and negative sets, utilizing a small number of training views. The approach incorporates an attention mechanism to identify objects, and utilizes the object's shape to predict its three-dimensional position, rather than relying on geometric features. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through experiments on a dataset of real-world scenes, achieving a 0.06 d$^2$-distance of 2.5° angle discrepancy for predicting rotation, and a 0.15 d$^2$-distance for predicting translation.

We propose a new method for managing the ratio of elastic coherent tunneling and crossed Andreev reflection processes in hybrid semiconductor-superconductor-ferromagnet structures. This can be achieved by utilizing the influence of subband Andreev bound states formed in the semiconductor region, where the structure's potential is tailored to produce these states. By fine-tuning the subband Andreev bound states, the tunneling and CAR processes can be independently managed.

Magnetic reconnection is a widespread process in nature that can quickly accelerate particles due to rapid changes in the magnetic field. However, the standard particle acceleration theory doesn't fully account for observed particle distributions, suggesting the need for an additional mechanism to explain the phenomenon. We propose that pitch-angle scattering, resulting from the changing magnetic field, can significantly influence particle behavior. By combining this pitch-angle scattering with the standard particle acceleration process, the distribution of particles can be accurately predicted, effectively incorporating the effects of both processes.

The Standard Model's scalar sector is currently the most incomplete part of our knowledge on e+e- physics. This study assesses the potential of using the $e+e- \to Zh$ process at future colliders to investigate expanded scalar sectors, specifically to reach scalar masses up to 1 TeV. Our findings show that the ILC at the 100 TeV energy level with 10 ab^-1 luminosity can achieve sensitivity to expanded scalar sectors with precision of around 0.3%. This precision is contingent upon a precise measurement of Z boson mass and weak gauge boson properties. This high level of sensitivity is due to the fact that the $e+e- \to Zh$ process is not affected by scalar couplings. This high level of sensitivity is also due to the fact that the process is not affected by scalar couplings. This is in contrast to other processes, such as Higgs decay into photons, which is affected by scalar couplings. Our study also shows that the potential of expanded scalar sectors is not limited to precision of 0.3%. We also consider the possibility of using $e+e- \to Zh$ at lower energies, 250 GeV and 500 GeV, which can achieve even higher precision, up to 0.05% and 0.01%. This is due to the fact that the cross section of the process is higher at lower energies, which can provide more statistical accuracy. This is also why

The combined numerical radius of a matrix is defined as the maximum value of the norms of its singular value decomposition and the absolute value of its off-diagonal entries in a specific order. This paper proves the differentiability of this quantity with respect to some specific matrices, while also investigating its subdifferential. The authors then apply these results to the spectral value.

The cryptocurrency industry is rapidly expanding, with a market capitalization of over 
$3 trillion USD. The widespread use of cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, and
Altcoins has led to a significant increase in the number of cryptocurrency users.
However, due to the inherent characteristics of blockchain technology, such as decentralization
and openness, the security of users' financial transactions and sensitive information is often
compromised, resulting in potential identity theft, money laundering, and loss of funds.
To mitigate these security risks, we propose a cutting-edge, decentralized, and
cryptocurrency-agnostic solution to enhance the confidentiality of users' financial
transactions, utilizing a complex algorithm that combines multiple consensus mechanisms.
Our solution is designed to be adaptable to various use cases, including credit card
transactions, without requiring modifications to existing payment systems.

This research introduces novel mathematical concepts to analyze stochastic processes and nonlinear systems with dynamic randomness. It focuses on a specific type of stochastic function, known as a stochastic mapping, which exhibits one-to-one correspondence and is invariant to inverse mapping. The study introduces a measure for evaluating the regularity of such stochastic mappings, employing correlation theory, and then examines their impact on complex nonlinear systems with allocated and interacting random elements. The analysis highlights the role of these mappings in both natural and engineered systems, particularly in processes like heat transfer and heat conduction, where exchange rates between local and neighboring states are described. The method's relevance to physical systems is demonstrated through applications, such as the Boltzmann collision term, the inverse Chapman-Enskog method, and the statistical mechanics of gas particles.

Our investigation focused on the ignition characteristics of high-pressure He, H2, and O2 mixtures within a cylindrical glass vessel sealed with quartz windows, with a maximum capacity of 1.6 L. Utilizing a focused laser beam from a Nd:YAG laser system (1,060 nm, 10 ns pulses with up to 20 J energy), we examined ignition thresholds in the presence of ambient air (20% He, 5% H2, 75% O2 by volume) at various pressures (0.1-100 kPa). The results revealed that an unfocused laser beam failed to ignite the gas mixture, with our data indicating a threshold energy of around 0.5 J per 10 cm3 at 50 kPa.

In real-world image segmentation tasks, it is crucial to pay equal attention to object areas and their boundaries. This is particularly true for medical image segmentation applications, where boundaries are vital for making accurate diagnoses. However, current deep learning-based image segmentation techniques often focus more on object areas while neglecting their boundaries. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new approach called the Boundary-Conscious Segmentation Network (BNet). This approach enables a unified representation of object areas and their boundaries using a single deep learning model. We also develop a loss function to guide the model to capture detailed information about object areas and their boundaries. We test the performance of BNet by applying it to image segmentation tasks and achieve better results compared to state-of-the-art techniques.

Existing driver communication systems are limited by design, prioritizing information transmission over user needs. To address this, we developed a new system that allows drivers and automated vehicles to collaborate effectively. By considering the importance of context, we designed a natural language-based interaction model that enables intuitive driver input and interpretation. Furthermore, we created a knowledge base that provides actionable information through simple, clear language. Our research demonstrates the practical application of our framework through a sample use case, where driver shift requests are clearly understood and responded to.

The movement of cold particles that don't interact with one another is studied in this research. We look at how these particles behave in different forms, such as two-dimensional squares and three-dimensional spheres, and use mathematical models to find the distribution of particles as time passes. We also consider how particles might be influenced and calculate how long it would take for these particles to reach a state of equilibrium. Notably, the distribution of one particular type of particle is unique, depending on the direction of movement limited only by the symmetries of the shapes in question.

In a model of a spherically symmetric, time-independent potential based on the Schrödinger equation, we investigate the properties of metastable states. These states have no resonance edges and exist in finite, discrete sets, which we study at each energy level. At the point where each energy level is fully occupied, the discrete set reaches its maximum size. By examining the asymptotic behavior of the potential, we demonstrate that a typical state in this discrete set exhibits certain characteristic properties, which depend on whether the potential is short-range or long-range.

The IRIS satellite's high-resolution spectra have significantly advanced our understanding of the solar atmosphere, particularly in flare-related events. The suborbital spacecraft's rapid spectral coverage has enabled researchers to study the dynamics of plasma formation and coronal formation conditions during these occurrences. In a recent flare event, which took place on August 21, 2016, the Si IV 1390.8 Angstrom emission showed a sudden increase in intensity, which was captured by the JAXA's IRIS2 and followed by a substantial decrease in about 5 minutes. The initial enhancement was characterized by a broadened line, indicating the formation of hot plasma. The rapid recovery was attributed to the cooling of the plasma. The location of the flare was identified as the footpoint of a loop with a temperature of about 10,000 Kelvin. The observed Si IV emission at the loop's footpoint was found to be influenced by the downflow of hot plasma from the corona. The results of this study have implications for understanding the formation of hot corona during solar flares.

We investigate the impact of a time-dependent axion field on the CP behavior of QCD, revealing that in the presence of an instanton, the CP violation rate is influenced by a balance of the QCD scale and the axion mass, and does not solely depend on instanton effects. This discovery has implications for the axion's role in the universe, and specifically its role in the axion dark matter formation process, which may be determined by a combination of the QCD scale and the axion mass rather than solely the axion mass. Additionally, our findings indicate that in the axion-fermion model, the axion's CP violation parameter must be greater than the QCD scale divided by the axion mass to avoid a conflict with experimental data.

The impact of the spatial distribution of energy deposited by an ion on the critical angle for nuclear stopping in thin films is significant. As a narrow beam of ions impinges a solid target, the energy is initially deposited in a focused manner, resulting in a non-Gaussian energy distribution. This is particularly evident in the case of elastic recoil collimation, where the spatial distribution of energy is even more pronounced than that of the recoiled atoms. This disparity in the critical angles for elastic and nuclear stopping further underscores the importance of accounting for the non-Gaussian nature of ion beam-induced energy deposition.

We introduce a novel approach, referred to as source code anti-cheating, that enables the execution of source code through the routing method, a cutting-edge quantum computing technique. To showcase its functionality, a C# console application is developed and demonstrated, including a simple calculator feature. Notably, the integration of source code is a groundbreaking achievement in the realm of quantum computing, as this innovation has the potential to significantly accelerate the integration of classical and quantum systems.

In the past, the investigation of automorphic functions via Dirichlet's theorem has been well-documented. Specifically, the values of automorphic functions at even integers have been previously examined. This study, however, focuses on a different aspect by exploring their values at all integers. We achieve this by leveraging a method rooted in Stechkin's theory of complete convergence. To apply this theory effectively, the creation of a suitable majorant series is essential. The majoration in our case is made possible by employing the van der Waay summation, which has been extensively documented in the literature.

This article explores the potential of forming a subgroup in a semigroup near to a specific subset of the semigroup. A semigroup S with an involution'fixes the form of elements within it, determined by the laws governing S and the definition of involution. A semigroup near to a subset A in S is a subset B in S where every element in A has a counterpart in S. We establish several results on near subgroups in semigroups featuring an involution, including semigroups in a particular class of semigroups 'S'. In these semigroups, the forms of elements are determined by monogenic subgroups. We demonstrate that a subset A in S is a set of generators for a semigroup near A if and only if A contains a full monogenic subsemigroup. A subset A in S is a semigroup if it contains the identity element and is equal to its own inverse. We prove that a semigroup near A in S is a semigroup if and only if A is a semigroup near A in S. We also find that a subset A in S is a semigroup if and only if A is a semigroup near A in S. A subset A in S is a left-right semigroup if it follows the left-right semigroup laws. We find that a left-right semigroup near A in S is a semigroup near A in S. A subset A in S is a right-left semigroup if it follows the right-left

We propose a new type of MCMCMC algorithm, log-concave grid (LCG), for estimating log-concave probability densities. LGC is an improved version of the log-concave MCMCMC method but with a significantly faster sampling speed, making it capable of handling large data sets.
